1.DialogueText: *Mary sits at her desk, slumped in her seat, anxiously watching the teacher hand back the recent test. The classroom buzzes with students talking as they glance at their grades. Mary catches a glimpse of her score: 43%. Her heart sinks.*

2.DialogueText: Mary, we’ll need to talk about this after class. That’s the fourth low score this semester. You’re capable of more.

3.DialogueText: Yeah… I know. I tried studying…?

4.DialogueText: Whoa, that bad? Don’t sweat it, though. It was a hard test.

5.DialogueText: You don’t get it. Mom’s gonna freak. I was so close this time…

6.DialogueText: Yeah, but, like, a 43? Close to what, exactly?

7.DialogueText: Okay, okay. Just... I can't go through another lecture.

8.DialogueText: Look, maybe she’ll go easy on you this time…? Anyway, are you still coming to Emma’s party tonight?

9.DialogueText: I dunno. Probably not. Mom’s already mad about my grades.

10.DialogueText: *Mary drags herself into the house, tossing her backpack by the door. Her mom is in the kitchen, prepping dinner. She looks up with a smile that quickly fades when she sees Mary’s face.*

11.DialogueText: Hey, Mary! How was school? How’d you do on that exam?

13.DialogueText: Not great? Mary, that’s the fourth bad grade this semester. What’s going on?

14.DialogueText: I dunno, Mom, it was hard! I studied for it.

15.DialogueText: Studied? Mary, if you’d been studying properly, this wouldn’t keep happening. You can’t just slide by with last-minute cramming.

16.DialogueText: Okay, fine, I get it. Can we please not do this again?

17.DialogueText: We have to, Mary! I’m not letting you go out tonight, that’s for sure. No party until your grades improve.

18.DialogueText: Are you kidding me? I really wanted to go…

19.DialogueText: Then maybe you should’ve put in more effort on that test. You’re staying in. End of discussion.

20.DialogueText: *turns away, heading to her room* Whatever…

21.DialogueText: *Mary slams her bedroom door, flopping onto her bed, staring at the ceiling. She feels trapped and frustrated, her mind buzzing with thoughts. She finally reaches for her laptop, opens it, and begins typing.*

timelinePuzzle.introText: Dangerous situations rarely start with the worst moment. They build step by step. Drag each scene into the timeline so Mary and Sophia’s stories run from first to last — and notice which choices keep them safer.
timelinePuzzle.introStep1Text: Each level is one story. The cards are moments from that story, mixed up.
timelinePuzzle.introStep2Text: Drag cards into the slots from FIRST to LAST. Correct cards lock in place.
timelinePuzzle.introStep3Text: Wrong cards bounce back. When the order is right, you get a short debrief.
timelinePuzzle.introNote: {{count}} stories. More points if you solve a level on the first check.
timelinePuzzle.poolHint: Drag, or tap a card then a slot
timelinePuzzle.poolEmpty: All scenes are on the timeline
timelinePuzzle.fillAll: Fill every slot before you check.
timelinePuzzle.incorrect: Not quite. Wrong cards came back — locked ones stay.
timelinePuzzle.rank_expert_text: You lined up every story with few retries ({{attempts}} checks total). You see how risk builds — and how help interrupts it.
timelinePuzzle.rank_sharp_text: Solid work across {{attempts}} checks. Review the lessons below: the early warning signs are the ones people skip.
timelinePuzzle.rank_training_text: You needed {{attempts}} checks this round. That’s fine — these stories are meant to feel messy until you sort them.
timelinePuzzle.safetyTitle: If something like this happens to you
timelinePuzzle.safety1: Don’t go alone to meet someone you only know online
timelinePuzzle.safety2: Never share your address, ID, or private photos with strangers
timelinePuzzle.safety3: Show weird invites and offers to a trusted adult
timelinePuzzle.safety4: Block, report, and keep screenshots. It’s never your fault
timelinePuzzle.helpline: In the Netherlands you can talk to De Kindertelefoon for free and anonymously on 0800‑0432, or get help with online abuse at helpwanted.nl.

level1.title: The secret party
level1.description: Line up how Mary handles a party invite from people she doesn’t know.
level1.lesson: Secret parties from strangers are recruitment lures. Asking a friend and a parent breaks the secrecy trap.
level1.step1: Mary gets an online invite to a secret party from people she doesn’t know.
level1.step2: She shows the invite to her friend and asks if they should go.
level1.step3: Her mom explains stranger-hosted parties are risky, so they don’t go.

level2.title: The fake scout
level2.description: Put the five steps in order: how Mary stops an online “modeling” stranger.
level2.lesson: Fake scouts rush trust and ask for personal details early. A trusted adult plus block-and-report stops it.
level2.step1: A stranger DMs Mary about a “modeling contract.”
level2.step2: They ask for personal details before any real contract exists.
level2.step3: Mary almost shares her address without checking who they are.
level2.step4: Her mother sees the chat and tells her to stop.
level2.step5: Mary blocks the stranger and reports it.

level3.title: The job flyer
level3.description: Order the seven steps that stop a fake job flyer at school.
level3.lesson: Too-good job offers can be traps. Checking with a teacher and a hotline protects more than one person.
level3.step1: Sophia spots a strange job flyer on the school board.
level3.step2: She reads it aloud and something feels off.
level3.step3: She shows the flyer to Mary for a second opinion.
level3.step4: Together they take it to their teacher.
level3.step5: The teacher calls the safety hotline to check it.
level3.step6: The hotline confirms the flyer is a scam.
level3.step7: The teacher removes it and posts a warning.

clickPuzzle.howToPlay: Click objects to interact. Collect items and use them together from your inventory.
clickPuzzle.objective: Help Mary escape by finding tools and solving each level's puzzle!
clickPuzzle.tapStart: (Click outside to start the escape mission)

emojiDecoder.introText: Traffickers and groomers rarely say what they want. They hide it in compliments, gifts, slang and emojis. You'll review real-style message threads Mary and her friends received, and work out what's really going on.
emojiDecoder.introStep1Text: Check the profile clues too: account age, mutual friends, what doesn't add up.
emojiDecoder.introStep2Text: Tap every message that's a manipulation tactic. Not every message is one, and false alarms cost points.
emojiDecoder.introStep3Text: Work out what an emoji combo really means in this conversation.
emojiDecoder.introStep4Text: Pick the safest response. Some answers are only partly right.
emojiDecoder.introNote: {{count}} cases. Points for every red flag you catch, every code you crack, and every safe move.
emojiDecoder.flagText: Tap each message that uses a manipulation tactic. Tap again to remove a flag.
emojiDecoder.flagHint: Not every message is dangerous. Flagging innocent messages costs a point each.
emojiDecoder.revealNoFlags: This thread had no red flags
emojiDecoder.falseAlarms_one: {{count}} false alarm: an innocent message you flagged.
emojiDecoder.falseAlarms_other: {{count}} false alarms: innocent messages you flagged.
emojiDecoder.rank_expert_text: You read between the lines like a pro. You spotted the tactics, cracked the codes, and made safe calls.
emojiDecoder.rank_sharp_text: You caught most of what was going on. Look at the tactics you missed: they're the ones that work best on people.
emojiDecoder.rank_training_text: These tactics are designed to feel normal. That's why they work. Go through the tactic file below and try again.
emojiDecoder.safetyTitle: If this ever happens to you
emojiDecoder.safety1: Don't reply, pay or send anything
emojiDecoder.safety4: Tell a trusted adult. It's never your fault
emojiDecoder.helpline: In the Netherlands you can talk to De Kindertelefoon for free and anonymously on 0800‑0432, or get help with online abuse at helpwanted.nl.

wordChoice.introText: Groomers and traffickers hide risk in ordinary-sounding words. You'll read short scenes Mary gets online, then pick the word that names what's really going on — or the safest move.
wordChoice.introStep1Text: A short context line sets up who is talking and why it matters.
wordChoice.introStep2Text: Choose the word that fits. Wrong options are meant to sound almost right.
wordChoice.introStep3Text: Every answer comes with a short debrief so the pattern sticks.
wordChoice.introNote: {{count}} questions. {{points}} points for each correct word.
wordChoice.previewContext: A new DM. Mary doesn’t know this person.
wordChoice.previewBefore: “Hang out tonight, no parents.” Traffickers use
wordChoice.previewAfter: to keep teens away from safe adults.
wordChoice.tip1: Ask: does this cut Mary off from adults or friends?
wordChoice.tip2: Urgency, secrecy, and “prove it” are common pressure tools.
wordChoice.tip3: If two words feel close, pick the one that names the risk.
wordChoice.rank_expert_text: You named {{correct}} of {{total}} correctly. You can tell when “nice” language is actually a trap.
wordChoice.rank_sharp_text: You got {{correct}} of {{total}}. Review the tactics you missed — those are the ones that sound the most normal.
wordChoice.rank_training_text: {{correct}} of {{total}} this round. These words are designed to feel ordinary. That’s why the practice matters.
wordChoice.safetyTitle: If this ever happens to you
wordChoice.safety1: Don’t reply, pay, or send anything
wordChoice.safety4: Tell a trusted adult. It’s never your fault
wordChoice.helpline: In the Netherlands you can talk to De Kindertelefoon for free and anonymously on 0800‑0432, or get help with online abuse at helpwanted.nl.

dangerWord.introText: Risky messages hide the trap in ordinary phrases. Tap every chunk that is a red flag — secrecy, urgency, gifts, private apps, location, personal data. Not every phrase is dangerous. False alarms cost points.
dangerWord.introStep1Text: Check the handle and the setup. Something may already feel off.
dangerWord.introStep2Text: Tap whole risky phrases, not random little words. Tap again to unflag.
dangerWord.introStep3Text: See what you caught, what you missed, and which picks were innocent.
dangerWord.introNote: {{count}} messages. +{{hit}} per catch, −{{cost}} per false alarm.
dangerWord.flagText: Tap each phrase that uses a manipulation tactic.
dangerWord.flagHint: Skip normal greetings and small talk. Flagging innocent phrases costs a point.
dangerWord.revealNoFlags: This message had no red flags
dangerWord.falseAlarms_one: {{count}} false alarm: an innocent phrase you flagged.
dangerWord.falseAlarms_other: {{count}} false alarms: innocent phrases you flagged.
dangerWord.rank_expert_text: You read past the friendly wrapping and caught the real asks. That skill keeps people safer.
dangerWord.rank_sharp_text: You caught a lot. Review the misses — those phrases are built to feel normal.
dangerWord.rank_training_text: These lines are designed to sound ordinary. Use the tactic file below and try again.
dangerWord.safetyTitle: If this ever happens to you

flashCards.introText: These aren’t baby safety slogans. Each card drops you into a messy teen scenario, then a claim that sounds smart, polite, or “realistic.” Call the bluff — or get baited.
flashCards.introStep1Text: Discord, deepfakes, gift debt, fake jobs — notice what’s being sold as logic.
flashCards.introStep2Text: True or false. The dangerous answers usually feel mature.
flashCards.introStep3Text: Flip for why it works on people your age — then keep a streak.
flashCards.introNote: {{count}} cards. +{{hit}} per hit, +{{bonus}} streak bonus from {{at}} in a row.
flashCards.previewLine1: Send one more pic to buy silence?
flashCards.previewLine2: Months on Discord = not a stranger?
flashCards.claimHint: True or false — the trap often sounds like strategy.
flashCards.rank_expert_text: {{hits}} of {{total}} correct, best streak {{streak}}. You can name the tricks behind the claims.
flashCards.rank_sharp_text: {{hits}} of {{total}} correct, best streak {{streak}}. Review the concepts that felt “almost true.”
flashCards.rank_training_text: {{hits}} of {{total}} correct, best streak {{streak}}. Use the file below — myths are designed to feel safe.

flashCards.safety2: Screenshot the messages and keep the evidence
flashCards.safety4: Tell a trusted adult. It’s never your fault

whoToTrust.introText: Each case hides a real pressure trick — secrecy, fake jobs, gift debt, photo tests. Study the clues (they won’t spoil the answer), pick who Mary should turn to, then learn the name of the trick.
whoToTrust.introStep1Text: Notice who wants secrecy, speed, gifts, or private chats — and who Mary already knows offline.
whoToTrust.introStep2Text: Cards show facts, not labels. Sometimes a friend is good support — and an adult is still safer.
whoToTrust.introStep3Text: Best scores full points. Partly safe scores less. After each pick you’ll get a plain-language explainer.
whoToTrust.introNote: {{count}} cases. +{{best}} for best, +{{partly}} for partly safe.

wordScramble.introText: Each scene hides a safety word in scrambled letters — sometimes with decoys that don’t belong. Build the word, then choose what Mary should do next.
wordScramble.introStep1Text: A short DM or situation sets the context. Use the clue if you’re stuck.
wordScramble.introStep2Text: Tap letter tiles into the slots. Extra decoy letters must stay in the tray.
wordScramble.introStep3Text: After you crack the word, choose the safest next step. Some answers are only partly right.
wordScramble.introStep4Text: Wrong checks and hints cost points. Solving clean keeps your streak alive.
wordScramble.introNote: {{count}} cases. Points for the word and for Mary’s move.
wordScramble.previewContext: They keep pushing after Mary said no.
wordScramble.tip1: Threat words name the trap. Action words name what Mary should do.
wordScramble.tip2: If a letter feels spare, it may be a decoy — leave it in the tray.
wordScramble.tip3: A hint locks one correct letter in place, but costs points.
wordScramble.keyboardHint: Keyboard: type letters, Backspace to undo, Enter to check.
wordScramble.rank_expert_text: You built {{solved}} words and kept a streak of {{streak}}. You can name the trap and the exit.
wordScramble.rank_sharp_text: {{solved}} words cracked, best streak {{streak}}. Review the ones that needed hints — those patterns are designed to confuse.
